stem: State **five** features of the Batista regime.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Batista took power in a coup in 1952 and ruled as a dictator; he repressed opponents and censored the press; his government was corrupt and linked to casinos and US organised crime; there was great inequality and rural poverty; and the economy depended on the USA.

stem: Explain the domestic results of the Cuban Revolution between 1959 and 1961.

points.description: Identifies land reform (May 1959).
Explains that large estates were broken up and land went to co-operatives, the state and peasants.
Identifies nationalisation (1960).
Explains that US and Cuban companies, banks and sugar mills were taken over, ending foreign control.
Identifies the literacy campaign / health and education, and loss of political freedom.
Explains: illiteracy fell sharply; but elections were not held, critics jailed and many Cubans emigrated.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Agrarian Reform Law of May 1959 broke up large estates, giving land to co-operatives, the state and peasants. In 1960 the government nationalised American and Cuban companies, banks and sugar mills, ending foreign control of the economy. The 1961 literacy campaign sent volunteers to teach adults to read, and free education and healthcare were extended. But political freedom ended: elections were not held, opposition papers were closed, critics were jailed, and many middle-class Cubans fled to the USA.

hints: Consider land, business, social services and political rights.

stem: Explain **two** reasons why Cuba became an ally of the Soviet Union after 1959.

points.description: Identifies the conflict with the USA over nationalisation.
Explains that the USA responded with an embargo, so Cuba needed a new market for sugar and a source of oil.
Identifies Soviet offers of trade and aid (1960 sugar-for-oil agreement) / protection.
Explains that the USSR wanted an ally near the USA and offered protection against invasion (Bay of Pigs).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: First, Castro's nationalisation of American property led the USA to stop buying Cuban sugar and impose an embargo, so Cuba needed new markets and a source of oil. Second, the USSR offered a trade agreement in 1960 exchanging oil for sugar, and later weapons and protection, because it wanted an ally close to the USA; after the Bay of Pigs invasion this protection became vital.

hints: Think about sugar, oil and fear of invasion.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — the memories of a fictional peasant woman from the Sierra Maestra, recorded in 1979 (invented for this question)

> Before the revolution my children had no school and no doctor. When the bearded ones came to the mountains, they paid for our pigs and their doctor treated my husband's fever. The soldiers of Batista only came to burn houses. After the triumph a young teacher lived in our hut for a whole year, and now I can write my own name.

**Source B** — a letter from a fictional Cuban lawyer who left for Miami, written in 1962 (invented for this question)

> I fought against Batista too. But Fidel promised elections and gave us firing squads. My newspaper was closed, my brother is in prison, and our property was taken. A revolution that makes half the professionals of Havana flee is not freedom; it is a new dictatorship.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What can you learn from Source A about why the guerrillas won rural support?

points.description: They paid for food / treated the sick.
Batista's soldiers burned houses (reprisals).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far do Sources A and B disagree about the results of the revolution?

points.description: A: positive results (education, healthcare, literacy).
B: negative results (no elections, executions, censorship, confiscation).
Agreement: both opposed Batista / accept the old regime was bad.
Judgement: they disagree mainly because they focus on different results.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why do these two sources give such different views of the revolution? Use the sources and your own knowledge.

points.description: Social position: A a poor rural woman who gained schooling and healthcare.
Social position: B a middle-class professional who lost property and freedom.
Own knowledge supports A: literacy campaign 1961, free healthcare, land reform.
Own knowledge supports B: executions of Batista officials, no elections, closed newspapers, emigration.
Timing/purpose: A recorded in 1979 (perhaps for an official account); B written in exile in 1962.
Judgement: both are accurate about different groups.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sources differ mainly because the writers were affected differently. The peasant woman in Source A was poor and rural; she gained schooling, a doctor and literacy, and my own knowledge confirms the literacy campaign of 1961 and the spread of free healthcare and land reform. The lawyer in Source B was a middle-class professional who lost his newspaper and property, and my knowledge confirms that elections were not held, Batista officials were executed, opposition papers were closed and many professionals fled to Miami. Their circumstances also differ: A was recorded in 1979, perhaps for an account approved by the government, while B was written by an angry exile in 1962. Both are accurate about the experiences of their own group, so together they show that the revolution brought social gains at the cost of political freedom.

parts.explanation: Explain differences using provenance and knowledge.

hints: Each writer saw a different side of the revolution; think about who they were.

Supported judgement.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Batista's weaknesses were very important. His regime was corrupt and repressive, so it had little support outside the wealthy and the army. The army was large but poorly motivated, and its brutal reprisals created more rebels. In March 1958 the USA stopped selling him weapons, damaging both his army and his authority, and his offensive that summer failed.

However, Castro's strengths turned these weaknesses into victory. The guerrillas survived in the Sierra Maestra by winning peasant support, used hit-and-run tactics to capture weapons, and spread their message through rebel radio and foreign journalists. An urban underground organised sabotage and strikes, and many groups opposed to Batista accepted Castro's leadership. Guevara's victory at Santa Clara in December 1958 made Batista flee.

Overall Batista's weaknesses created the opportunity, but without Castro's leadership and the guerrillas' skill the regime might have survived, so I only partly agree with the statement.

parts.explanation: Both sides and a supported judgement.

hints: In (b), weigh the guerrillas' strengths against Batista's weaknesses.
